summary: This note describes the parietal lobe, one of the four major lobes of the mammalian cerebral cortex, located above the temporal lobe and behind the frontal lobe and central sulcus. It covers the lobe's boundaries and subdivisions (postcentral gyrus, superior and inferior parietal lobules, intraparietal sulcus areas LIP, VIP, MIP and AIP), its roles in touch, spatial awareness, visuomotor control, and memory, and the clinical effects of lesions in the dominant and non-dominant hemispheres.
one_line: Overview of the parietal lobe's location, subdivisions, sensory and visuospatial functions, and clinical effects of damage.
key_facts: The parietal lobe is one of the four major lobes of the cerebral cortex in mammals.
The parietal lobe is positioned above the temporal lobe and behind the frontal lobe and central sulcus.
The primary somatosensory cortex is the postcentral gyrus (Brodmann area 3), immediately posterior to the central sulcus.
The posterior parietal cortex is subdivided into the superior parietal lobule (Brodmann areas 5 and 7) and the inferior parietal lobule (39 and 40), separated by the intraparietal sulcus.
The name parietal comes from the parietal bone, which derives from the Latin paries-, meaning "wall".
The posterior parietal cortex is often referred to as the dorsal stream of vision, called the "where" stream and the "how" stream.
The cortical homunculus (Latin: "little man") depicts body parts in proportion to how much somatosensory cortex is devoted to them.
A lesion commonly in the right superior or inferior parietal lobule leads to hemineglect.
The lateral intraparietal (LIP) area contains a map of neurons representing the saliency of spatial locations and attention to them, used for targeting eye movements.
The anterior intraparietal (AIP) area contains neurons responsive to shape, size, and orientation of objects to be grasped.
Gerstmann syndrome is characterized by acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation.
Amorphosynthesis is a loss of perception on one side of the body caused by a lesion in the parietal lobe, and the term was coined by D. Denny-Brown to describe patients he studied in the 1950s.
Bilateral damage to the inferior parietal lobe does not cause amnesia but diminishes memory strength and makes details of complex events harder to retrieve.
Apraxia was shaped as a concept by Hugo Liepmann about a hundred years ago and is predominantly a symptom of left brain damage.

entities.name: Parietal lobe
entities.role: subject of the note; one of the four major lobes of the cerebral cortex

entities.name: Central sulcus
entities.role: boundary separating the parietal lobe from the frontal lobe

entities.name: Parieto-occipital sulcus
entities.role: boundary separating the parietal and occipital lobes

entities.name: Lateral sulcus (sylvian fissure)
entities.role: most lateral boundary separating the parietal lobe from the temporal lobe

entities.name: Longitudinal fissure
entities.role: divides the two cerebral hemispheres

entities.name: Postcentral gyrus
entities.role: primary somatosensory cortical area (Brodmann area 3)

entities.name: Postcentral sulcus
entities.role: separates the postcentral gyrus from the posterior parietal cortex

entities.name: Superior parietal lobule
entities.role: subdivision of posterior parietal cortex (Brodmann areas 5 and 7), primary area of body or spatial awareness

entities.name: Inferior parietal lobule
entities.role: subdivision of posterior parietal cortex (Brodmann areas 39 and 40), primary area of body or spatial awareness

entities.name: Intraparietal sulcus (IPS)
entities.role: separates the superior and inferior parietal lobules; essential in guiding limb and eye movement

entities.name: Thalamus
entities.role: relays major skin sensory inputs to the parietal lobe

entities.name: Lateral intraparietal (LIP) area
entities.role: intraparietal area holding a map of spatial saliency and attention, used for eye movement targeting

entities.name: Ventral intraparietal (VIP) area
entities.role: intraparietal area receiving visual, somatosensory, auditory and vestibular input

entities.name: Medial intraparietal (MIP) area
entities.role: intraparietal area encoding the location of reach targets in eye-centered coordinates

entities.name: Anterior intraparietal (AIP) area
entities.role: intraparietal area with neurons responsive to shape, size and orientation of objects to be grasped

entities.name: Hugo Liepmann
entities.role: shaped the concept of apraxia about a hundred years ago

entities.name: D. Denny-Brown
entities.role: coined the term amorphosynthesis to describe patients he studied in the 1950s

entities.name: Gerstmann syndrome
entities.role: clinical condition characterized by acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation

entities.name: Bálint's syndrome
entities.role: clinical condition listed under bilateral hemisphere parietal lesions

entities.name: Amorphosynthesis
entities.role: loss of perception on one side of the body caused by a parietal lobe lesion
